newsitem.title: UK: Higher MEPC profit hit by exceptional cost.
newsitem.headline: Higher MEPC profit hit by exceptional cost.

text.p: British property group MEPC on Tuesday reported increased first half pre-tax profits of 75.7 million pounds ($124 million) which were all but wiped out by an exceptional charge.
But by cancelling interest rate swap agreements at a cost of 73.2 million pounds MEPC said it had substantially reduced future costs and predicted increased dividend cover for 1998 and beyond.
Analysts said there were no real surprises in the results, which got a subdued market reaction. MEPC shares were down 3.0 pence at 512.5 pence at 1150 GMT.

Mike Prew, property analyst at BZW, highlighted the interest rate swap provision, the prediction on dividend cover and the fact MEPC had sold properties at a 10 percent surplus to last September's valuations as the main points of interest in the results.

While Prew said the rest of the portfolio should see a greater increase and this would mean MEPC's net asset value (NAV) would be around 500 pence at the end of September, others were slightly less bullish suggesting an overall rise of eight percent and a NAV of 490 pence, compared with 450 pence in 1996.
MEPC chief executive James Tuckey told Reuters the group was well positioned to make the most of a market which was moving in its favour, although he warned there were signs of overheating.
This caution was inevitable given the experience of boom and bust in the late 1980s and early 1990s in the British property market, one analyst said.

While dismissing recent takeover talk surrounding MEPC, Tuckey said he would not be doing his duty to shareholders if he did not treat any approaches seriously, although he admitted the fall-out following the talks had been a distraction.
He said the firm, which in March announced it had ended merger talks with smaller rival Hammerson, was not talking to anyone at the moment and did not anticipate doing so.
MEPC said the scale of benefits from a merger with Hammerson would have been small and the financial effect would have diluted its earnings per share and reduced the dividends for its shareholders.
The second analyst said MEPC had successfully repelled any potential boarders for the time being by its management changes and financial restructuring.
"They have done as much as they can," he said.
And the appointment of Robert Ware as corporate development director could signal the group was actually looking at making its own acquisitions.

MEPC said it would maintain its dividend at 20 pence per share for 1997, announcing a maintained interim dividend of 5.25 pence. But it said the cancellation of the swap agreements would improve dividend cover in 1998 and subsequent years.
"We think profits will be strong enough for the dividend to be increased for the first time since 1991," one analyst said.
Tuckey said MEPC had made management changes, refocused its portfolio, reduced its debt cost and had a modest development programme in the pipeline.
"Its been an extremely active six months and we feel pretty confident with the outlook," he said.
But while he sees the property market continuing to improve for the next 18-24 months, Tuckey said he was acutely aware of its cyclical nature.
"A correction will come and we need to be prepared," he said. It was a legitimate question to ask if the market was overheating, he added.
The easy availability of credit from both British and overseas banks was a key factor in this, and one which banks needed to be wary of, Tuckey said.
Despite this caution, MEPC is involved in a development programme with over 300 million pounds of expenditure still to come in the next few years.
The firm has 164 million pounds for purchases and development in the pipeline for the second half.
While much of this is directed at the British market, particularly the leisure sector, MEPC also has schemes underway in Dallas in the U.S. and Brisbane, Australia.
Tuckey said he did not know if there was a "big deal" likely in the British property company sector but based on MEPC's experience of its talks with Hammerson, any likely cost savings were not great.
It was probably more correct to direct talk of rationalisation to the smaller companies, where cost savings might be greater, he added. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
